The Holocaust imagery is the most contested thing in it: the lampshade, the Jew linen, the soap and the gold filling are images of what the camps made of human bodies, and Plath uses them to describe what has been made of hers. The poem does not apologise for the comparison or explain it, and the last stanza refuses consolation altogether: the speaker does not rise into heaven but into appetite, 'and I eat men like air'. The poem's rhetoric is that of the stage, and it is worth being exact about the audience: the 'peanut-crunching crowd' is not a metaphor for readers but for the spectators of a miracle, and the speaker's complaint is that her suffering has been converted into a spectacle that pays. That is why the poem's revenge is also a claim about art: to 'eat men like air' is to become the thing that consumes rather than the thing consumed, and the closing image is deliberately less consoling than triumphant.
narrative_structure: Twenty-eight unrhymed tercets, mostly one sentence per stanza, with a refrain-like repetition of 'Herr' in the closing addresses and a movement from the public display of the first half to the private history of the second and the revenge of the last three stanzas; the poem has no stanza breaks beyond the tercet, so the escalation is continuous.
literary_form: Poem (twenty-eight tercet stanzas in free verse)
meter_and_prosody: Very short lines, often of two or three words, with heavy internal rhyme and assonance ('Do I terrify?', 'the peanut-crunching crowd'); a diction that mixes the circus barker, the medical report and the nursery rhyme; direct address used as a weapon; and a use of proper names - Lazarus, God, Lucifer - that keeps the poem at the scale of myth even when it is most confessional.
historical_context: Written between 23 and 29 October 1962 at Court Green, in the weeks after the break-up of Plath's marriage and in the middle of the sequence of poems, including 'Daddy' and 'Ariel', that made her late manner; first published in Ariel (London: Faber and Faber, 1965). Its 'Herr Doktor' belongs to the German and Austrian doctors of Plath's biography - her father Otto Plath's German origins and her own memories of the American hospital in which she was treated after her 1953 suicide attempt. The poem's Holocaust imagery was written in the knowledge of the Eichmann trial of 1961, and the argument about its propriety began almost as soon as the poem was published.
literary_significance: 'Lady Lazarus' is one of the two or three poems by which Plath is known, and its closing lines are among the most recognised in twentieth-century English poetry; it is central to the feminist criticism of the 1970s that made Plath a public figure, to the study of confessional writing, and to the continuing argument about the uses of Holocaust imagery in postwar literature.
bibliographical_notes: Written 23-29 October 1962; first published in Ariel (London: Faber and Faber, 1965); reprinted in The Collected Poems (1981) and in Ariel: The Restored Edition (2004). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is survival as a performance, in which the survivor is paid in attention and the audience is complicit in the death it comes to see. The second is the ownership of a body and of a case history, argued in the addresses to 'Herr Doktor' and 'Herr Enemy': the doctors, the husband and the god are versions of the same proprietor. The third is the use of the Holocaust as a figure for the woman's condition, which is the poem's most argued-over decision and the reason it is now taught as much for its politics as for its craft. The fourth is rebirth itself, drawn from the Gospel of John and from the phoenix, and deliberately parodic: what rises is not the soul but the body's appetite.
summary: The speaker begins by boasting that she has 'done it again', once every ten years, and describes herself as 'a sort of walking miracle' with skin 'bright as a Nazi lampshade' and a face 'a featureless, fine / Jew linen'. She invites the crowd to 'peel off the napkin', asks 'Do I terrify?', and catalogues her body - nose, eye pits, teeth, sour breath - before promising that the flesh the grave ate will be at home on her again and she will be 'a smiling woman'. She is 'only thirty' and has, like a cat, nine times to die: 'This is Number Three.' The 'peanut-crunching crowd' shoves in to see her unwrapped 'hand and foot', the 'big strip tease'; she displays her hands and knees and insists that she is 'the same, identical woman'. The first death, at ten, was 'an accident'; the second she meant, rocking shut 'as a seashell' while they called and picked the worms off her 'like sticky pearls'. Then the poem's most famous turn: 'Dying / Is an art, like everything else. / I do it exceptionally well.' She does it 'so it feels like hell', 'so it feels real', and says, 'I guess you could say I've a call.' The comeback in broad day is 'the theatrical' - 'A miracle!' - and there is a charge for the eyeing of her scars, for the hearing of her heart, for 'a piece of my hair or my clothes'. The final movement addresses 'Herr Doktor' and 'Herr Enemy' - 'I am your opus, / I am your valuable, / The pure gold baby / That melts to a shriek' - and passes through ash and bone ('A cake of soap, / A wedding ring, / A gold filling') to the last three stanzas, in which she warns 'Herr God, Herr Lucifer' to beware and rises from the ash with her red hair to eat men like air.
critical_context: The criticism is divided between readings that take the poem as a triumphant assertion of female survival and readings that find in it a dangerous appropriation of the language of the camps; biographical critics have traced the 'three deaths' to the 1953 overdose and to the earlier accident and illness, and formal critics have read the tercets as a parody of the hymn. Seamus Heaney's charge that Plath's Holocaust imagery is 'a poetry of the will' and the defences of later feminist critics remain the terms of the argument.
research_notes: No periodical printing before Ariel was established from the sources consulted; the 1965 date is the date of first publication in book form. The BBC recording of October 1962 includes lines omitted from the printed text, and the published version is the one recorded here.

title: Ariel
description: 'Ariel' was written on 27 October 1962, Plath's thirtieth birthday, and first published in Ariel (Faber and Faber, 1965), the collection that took its title from it. Ten tercets and a single closing line describe a dawn horse ride: 'Stasis in darkness. / Then the substanceless blue / Pour of tor and distances.' The rider becomes one with the horse, then with the drive itself - 'God's lioness', 'White / Godiva', 'the arrow, / The dew that flies / Suicidal' - and the poem ends in 'the red / Eye, the cauldron of morning'. It is Plath's most concentrated lyric and the one that gives its name to the whole of her late work.
plot_or_argument: 'Ariel' compresses the whole of Plath's late manner into thirty-one lines. It begins with a stasis that is also an unmaking - darkness, then a blue with no substance - and every stage of the ride is a further shedding: the rider loses the horse's neck, then her dead 'stringencies', then her body, until the only thing left is motion. The poem's pronouns matter: 'I cannot catch' and 'I unpeel' give way to 'And I / Am the arrow', a predication rather than an action, so that the self at the end is not a rider but the ride. The images are drawn from the stable, the harvest and the Christian martyrdom - God's lioness, Godiva, the dew, the red eye - and they are held in tercets whose line breaks keep interrupting the sentence at the point of greatest speed. The famous 'Suicidal' is both literal and descriptive of the drive: the poem was written on Plath's birthday, five months after her separation, and it is hard not to read the line biographically; but within the poem it names the impersonality the whole ride has been reaching for. The poem's extraordinary economy is worth stating plainly: in thirty-one lines it moves through five distinct states - stasis, the blue of distance, the merging with the horse, the shedding of the rider's body, and the final identification with the arrow - and it does so without a single connective to explain the transitions. Plath wrote it on her thirtieth birthday, and the coincidence of the birthday with the poem's theme of rebirth has governed its reception; but the poem's own logic is not the logic of an autobiography. It is the logic of a ride, in which the rider's will is progressively handed over to the animal's speed, and the last line arrives at a colour - red - that is also the colour of the sun and of blood, and a word, 'cauldron', that belongs to the kitchen and to witchcraft at once.
narrative_structure: Ten unrhymed tercets and a single closing line, each stanza a breath-length unit with the sentence running across the breaks; the movement is chronological (darkness to sunrise) but the stages are metamorphic rather than narrative, and the final line stands alone as the arrival the whole poem has been riding towards.
literary_form: Poem (ten tercets with a closing single line)
meter_and_prosody: Extremely compressed free verse with a strong, almost chant-like rhythm; heavy alliteration and assonance ('substanceless blue', 'Pivot of heels and knees'); ellipsis and parataxis, with verbs often omitted; a diction that is archaic and liturgical ('God's lioness', 'Godiva', 'stringencies') set against the physical detail of the ride; and a closing image of pure colour.
historical_context: Written on 27 October 1962, Plath's thirtieth birthday, at Court Green; 'Ariel' was the name of the horse she rode at a riding school on Dartmoor, and Ted Hughes recorded that she had ridden a bolting horse as a student at Cambridge. The poem was first published in Ariel (London: Faber and Faber, 1965) and gives the collection its title; in the restored edition of 2004 it stands in the middle of Plath's own sequence, where she had placed it.
literary_significance: 'Ariel' is the poem that named the most influential posthumous collection in modern English poetry, and its title has become the shorthand for Plath's late manner; it is a set text in the teaching of twentieth-century lyric and the poem most often used to demonstrate her mastery of the short, driven stanza.
bibliographical_notes: Written 27 October 1962; first published in Ariel (London: Faber and Faber, 1965); reprinted in The Collected Poems (1981) and in Ariel: The Restored Edition (2004). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the dissolution of the self into pure motion, which the poem pursues through a series of metamorphoses from rider to lioness to Godiva to arrow to dew. The second is the landscape of Dartmoor as an image of that dissolution: the tors, the furrow, the berries, the 'cauldron of morning' are all forms of the same energy. The third is rebirth, and the poem is deliberately ambiguous about whether the rider's flight is a release or a death; 'the child's cry / Melts in the wall' is the one domestic sound in the poem and it is swallowed. Read with 'Lady Lazarus' and 'Daddy', 'Ariel' completes a trio in which the self is murdered, resurrected and finally dissolved, and it is the most impersonal of the three.
summary: The poem opens in stillness and darkness, then in the 'substanceless blue' of distance and the 'Pour of tor and distances' - the tors of Dartmoor. The rider and horse grow one: 'God's lioness, / How one we grow, / Pivot of heels and knees! - The furrow // Splits and passes, sister to / The brown arc / Of the neck I cannot catch'. Berries cast dark hooks, 'Black sweet blood mouthfuls'; something else 'hauls me through air - / Thighs, hair; / Flakes from my heels'. The rider becomes 'White / Godiva', unpeeling 'Dead hands, dead stringencies', then 'Foam to wheat, a glitter of seas'; the child's cry 'melts in the wall'; and the last four stanzas give the poem its terrible speed: 'And I / Am the arrow, // The dew that flies / Suicidal, at one with the drive / Into the red // Eye, the cauldron of morning.'
critical_context: Readings divide between the biographical - the birthday ride as a figure of rebirth or of suicide - and the formal, which attend to the tercets, the ellipses and the metamorphic series; feminist critics have read the poem's 'Godiva' and its dissolution of the female body as a critique of the spectacle of the woman, and the poem's relation to Hughes's own horse poems has been much discussed.
research_notes: The poem's title is also the title of the collection, which is why the record is for the poem and not the book; no periodical printing before Ariel was established from the sources consulted. 'Ariel' was a working title of the collection too, and Plath's manuscript is titled Ariel and other poems.

title: Daddy
description: 'Daddy' was written on 12 October 1962, a day after 'The Applicant' and one month after Plath's separation from Ted Hughes, and first published in Ariel (Faber and Faber, 1965). Its sixteen quintains address the father who died when she was eight, and they move through idolatry, German and Polish memory, the Nazi and the Jew, the blackboard and the black telephone, to the vampire staked in the heart and the last line, 'Daddy, daddy, you bastard, I'm through.' The rhyme is carried by the long 'oo' vowel that closes most of the stanzas, so that the poem sounds like a nursery rhyme while it performs a symbolic murder.
plot_or_argument: 'Daddy' is a poem of exorcism built on a child's chant. Its engine is the long 'oo' rhyme - shoe, do, Achoo, you, blue, two, through - which recurs in most of the sixteen quintains and gives the poem the momentum of a skipping game even at its most violent. Against that music Plath sets a sequence of increasingly extreme identifications: the father as black shoe, as statue, as Nazi, as vampire; the daughter as foot, as Jew, as the one who made a model of him and married it. The poem's controversial middle - the camps, the swastika, 'Every woman adores a Fascist' - is not decoration but the logic of the child's overestimation: if the father was everything, he was also the state, the army and the executioner, and the only way to be free of him is to make him a monster and then kill the monster. The last movement turns from the father to the husband who replaced him, and the closing 'I'm through' is at once a telephone disconnection and a declaration that the poem is finished and the mourning with it. The poem's formal signature is the vowel rhyme, and it is worth naming what it does: because the rhyme is carried by a single sound and not by a pattern of consonants, the stanzas feel both closed and endlessly repeatable, like the verses of a counting-out game, and the reader is carried from one enormity to the next on a rhythm that will not let them stop to object. That is the poem's ethical problem and its technical achievement at the same moment. The sixteen quintains are also a history in miniature: the father's death, the town in Poland, the train to the camps, the photograph on the blackboard, the suicide attempt at twenty, the husband made in the father's image, and the stake through the heart - each a scene the poem will not explain, arranged in the order a child might remember them rather than the order an analyst would reconstruct.
narrative_structure: Sixteen unrhymed quintains (the first and last of five lines, with an extra section break before the final three stanzas), held together by a single vowel rhyme that returns at the end of most stanzas; the movement is from the father's death to the attempt to recover him to the husband who replaces him, and the last three stanzas stage the exorcism.
meter_and_prosody: Short trimeter and dimeter lines in quintains, with a rhyme scheme carried by the 'oo' vowel rather than by exact rhyme; a diction that mixes the nursery ('Achoo', 'black shoe') with German and with the machinery of war; heavy repetition ('back, back, back', 'ich, ich, ich, ich'); and a tone that shifts without transition between the child's and the executioner's.
historical_context: Written on 12 October 1962 at Court Green, a day after 'The Applicant' and a month after Hughes's departure; first published in Ariel (London: Faber and Faber, 1965). Otto Plath, born in Grabow in Prussia, died of undiagnosed diabetes in November 1940, when Plath was eight; the poem's Polish town and its German are his, and the 'gipsy ancestress' is a family story. Plath read 'Daddy' on the BBC in October 1962, and it is the poem most often cited in the argument about the editing of Ariel.
literary_significance: 'Daddy' is the most famous poem Plath wrote and one of the most anthologised poems in English of the twentieth century; it is a set text wherever confessional poetry is taught, and its use of Holocaust imagery has made it a permanent case in the ethics of poetic metaphor.
bibliographical_notes: Written 12 October 1962; first published in Ariel (London: Faber and Faber, 1965); reprinted in The Collected Poems (1981) and in Ariel: The Restored Edition (2004). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem's first subject is the dead father as the origin of the speaker's speech: the 'Ach, du', the stuck tongue and 'Ich, ich, ich, ich' are all about a language inherited from him and unusable without him. The second is the substitution of husband for father, which the poem presents not as a psychological thesis but as a deed - 'I made a model of you... And I said I do, I do.' The third is the Holocaust, used as the extreme vocabulary of absolute power, and the poem is now as often discussed for that decision as for its craft. The fourth is the nursery rhyme itself: 'Daddy' is a poem about the way a child's chant carries an adult's rage, and its formal genius is that the reader hears the chant before the rage.
summary: The first quintain establishes the address and the image: 'You do not do, you do not do / Any more, black shoe / In which I have lived like a foot / For thirty years, poor and white, / Barely daring to breathe or Achoo.' The second: 'Daddy, I have had to kill you. / You died before I had time', and the father is a 'Marble-heavy, a bag full of God, / Ghastly statue with one gray toe / Big as a Frisco seal'. The poem goes to the German tongue and the Polish town 'scraped flat by the roller / Of wars', to the father's 'Ach, du', and to the speaker's inability to speak: 'The tongue stuck in my jaw. / It stuck in a barb wire snare. / Ich, ich, ich, ich, / I could hardly speak.' Every German was the father, and the language 'an engine, an engine / Chuffing me off like a Jew', 'A Jew to Dachau, Auschwitz, Belsen'. The middle stanzas give the father as 'Panzer-man', 'Not God but a swastika', and the notorious line 'Every woman adores a Fascist'. Then the photograph on the blackboard, the cleft chin, the father as 'the black man who / Bit my pretty red heart in two'; the burial when she was ten, the attempted suicide at twenty ('And get back, back, back to you'), the glue that stuck her together; the model of the father made in a husband, 'A man in black with a Meinkampf look // And a love of the rack and the screw', and the marriage vow, 'And I said I do, I do.' The close cuts the black telephone off at the root, and ends: 'There's a stake in your fat black heart / And the villagers never liked you... Daddy, daddy, you bastard, I'm through.'
critical_context: The criticism is largely an argument about the Holocaust imagery: for some readers the swastika and the camps are the poem's justification, since they measure the child's absolutism; for others they are an appropriation that the poem never earns. Against that argument run the formal readings, which attend to the quintains and the vowel rhyme as a return of the nursery, and the biographical, which trace the black telephone and the 'model' to Plath's marriage. Robert Phillips's early reading of the poem as a metaphorical murder of the father's memory is still the starting point for most later accounts.
research_notes: No periodical printing before Ariel was established from the sources consulted; the 1965 date is the date of first publication in book form. The poem's German and its Polish town are given in the text; the biographical facts of Otto Plath's birth and death are recorded here from the encyclopaedic sources, not from the poem.

title: Words
description: 'Words' was written on 1 February 1963, ten days before Plath's death, and first published in Ariel (Faber and Faber, 1965) as the last poem in the 1965 text. Six quatrains compare words to the rings a stone makes in water, to the echo of hoof-beats, and finally to stars that are 'fixed and moving' and govern a life without being asked; it is the shortest and the most impersonal of her late poems, and it stands as her ars poetica.
plot_or_argument: 'Words' is a poem about what poems do after they are written, and it is unusually free of the confessional apparatus of Plath's other late work: there is no father, no husband and no hospital, only the axe, the sap, the horses and the stars. Its movement is a sequence of similes that get further away from the speaker - the axe-stroke is close and violent, the sap rises and weeps, the horses grow distant and silent, and the stars are fixed at the bottom of a pool. The last two quatrains abandon simile altogether and state the moral: words are 'fixed and moving', they do not answer, and they govern a life. Read as the poem Plath put last in the 1965 Ariel, it is a leave-taking of poetry written by a poet ten days from death, and it has often been read as her most serene statement about her own art.
narrative_structure: Six unrhymed quatrains, largely in trimeter and tetrameter, with each stanza a complete sentence or a pair of sentences and a movement of withdrawal from the axe to the stars; the poem's last line falls at the very end of the sentence it completes.
meter_and_prosody: Short, regular quatrains with an almost entirely end-stopped syntax; a diction drawn from woodwork, riding and astronomy rather than from the clinic; simile used as the poem's whole structure, then dropped for the last plain statements; and an absence of the first person that is unusual in Plath's late work.
historical_context: Written on 1 February 1963 at Fitzroy Road, London, ten days before Plath's death, and placed last in the 1965 Ariel, where it closes the collection; reprinted in The Collected Poems (1981). It is one of the poems of the final week, with 'Edge', 'Balloons' and 'Contusion', and it belongs to the winter sequence in which the earlier, driven manner gives way to a sparer one.
literary_significance: 'Words' is Plath's most quoted statement about poetry and the poem that critics use to argue that her late work is not only confessional; it closes the 1965 Ariel and is therefore the last word of the collection that made her reputation, and it is a standard anthology poem in the teaching of twentieth-century poetics.
bibliographical_notes: Written 1 February 1963; first published in Ariel (London: Faber and Faber, 1965), where it stands as the last poem of the 1965 text; reprinted in The Collected Poems (1981) and in Ariel: The Restored Edition (2004). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the autonomy of language: words, once written, are 'dry and riderless' and they act on the writer rather than for her. The second is the relation of the poem to the life that made it, which 'Words' figures as a pool in which the stars are both reflected and fixed. The third is silence, which the poem approaches through the dying fall of its images from axe to sap to hoof to stars. It is also, formally, a poem about form: the quatrains are so regular that the poem seems to have been found rather than made, which is exactly the condition it describes.
summary: The first quatrain sets the comparison: 'Axes / After whose stroke the wood rings, / And the echoes / Travel outward like horses.' The second: 'Then the sap rises, / Weeping like tears, like water / Striving to re-cover / The rock that is the centre.' The third turns to the approach of a rider: 'More silent than the tramp of horses, / And more distant than the storm, / The words dry and riderless, / And the hoof-taps of horses.' The fourth has the stars, 'fixed and moving', and the fifth and sixth close the poem with the stars 'governing a life' and the lines 'From the bottom of the pool, fixed stars / Govern a life.'
critical_context: Readings have treated 'Words' as an ars poetica, as a poem about the afterlife of the written text, and as a formal exercise in the plain style that Plath was moving towards in her last weeks; its position at the end of the 1965 Ariel has been read both as Hughes's elegiac framing and as a placing that Plath's own manuscript supports, since her restored sequence also ends with it.
research_notes: No periodical printing was established from the sources consulted; the 1965 date is the date of first publication in book form. Its place as the last poem of the 1965 Ariel is confirmed by the collection's contents list.

title: Child
description: 'Child' was written on 28 January 1963, two weeks before Plath's death, and was not printed in Ariel; it first appeared in Winter Trees (Faber and Faber, 1971). Eight lines address the child's 'clear eye' as 'the one absolutely beautiful thing', and the poem asks to fill it with 'color and ducks, / The zoo of the new', before closing on the single word 'Wringing' and the line 'Your clear eye is the one absolutely beautiful thing.' It is the last of Plath's poems about her children and the shortest of the Norton selections.
plot_or_argument: 'Child' is a poem of two rooms. The first is the child's eye, which the mother wants to fill with the names of flowers and animals; the second is the room they are actually in, with its dark ceiling and the mother's wringing hands. The poem's movement is from the wish to the admission, and its brevity is the point: there is no time, and no room, for anything between them. Plath wrote it on 28 January 1963, a fortnight before her death, and it belongs with 'Edge' and 'Words' to the last week's poems; the tenderness is undiminished and the despair is unargued, and the poem ends not on the child's eye but on the ceiling it is reflecting.
narrative_structure: Eight unrhymed short lines, run as two sentences across four and four, with the poem turning at 'not this troublous' and the last two lines falling into the dark ceiling; there is no stanza division, so the turn is carried entirely by syntax.
meter_and_prosody: Extremely short free-verse lines with a high proportion of monosyllables; a diction of flowers and animals ('snowdrop', 'Indian pipe', 'ducks') set against a diction of the sickroom ('troublous', 'Wringing', 'dark'); a single long sentence interrupted by a dash; and an almost entire absence of the figurative language that the rest of the late poems rely on.
historical_context: Written on 28 January 1963 at Fitzroy Road, London, two weeks before Plath's death, and not included in the 1965 Ariel; first published in Winter Trees (London: Faber and Faber, 1971) and reprinted in The Collected Poems (1981). Its subject is Plath's son Nicholas, born in January 1962, and it belongs to the last group of poems in which she wrote about her children.
literary_significance: 'Child' is the best known of Plath's poems about her children after 'Morning Song' and the one most often set beside it to show how far the two years between them had taken her; it is a standard anthology poem and its opening line is among the most quoted in her work.
bibliographical_notes: Written 28 January 1963; first published in Winter Trees (London: Faber and Faber, 1971) and reprinted in The Collected Poems (1981). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the failure of the imagination's gift: the mother wants to give the child a world of names and images, and what she has to give instead is her own 'troublous wringing of hands'. The second is infancy as an unmediated attention, the child as the only clear eye in the poem. The third is the relation of art to care - the mother's business is to fill the eye with 'the zoo of the new', and the poem is the record of her inability to do it. It is also, quietly, a poem about the material of poetry: the snowdrop, the Indian pipe and the 'little stalk' are the stock of a nature poem, and the poem is asking whether they can be given to a child or only written.
summary: The poem in full: 'Your clear eye is the one absolutely beautiful thing. / I want to fill it with color and ducks, / The zoo of the new // Whose name you meditate - / April snowdrop, Indian pipe, / Little // Stalk without wrinkle, / Pool in which images / Should be grand and classical, not this troublous // Wringing of hands, this dark / Ceiling without a star.' Its two sentences move from the child's eye as the one beautiful thing to the adult's 'troublous / Wringing of hands' and the 'dark / Ceiling without a star' that the child's eye is reflecting, and the poem's whole argument is carried by the contrast between the zoo of the new and the room in which it is being imagined.
critical_context: Critics have read 'Child' as a counterweight to the poems of maternal rage, as a poem about the impossibility of giving a child an unspoiled world, and as a late instance of Plath's turn to the plain style; its relation to 'Morning Song', written two years earlier about the same child, has been the starting point for most accounts of her late development.
research_notes: The poem is not in the 1965 Ariel, which is why its first publication is 1971 and not 1965; the 1971 date of the list is therefore the date of first publication in book form, not of composition. The Winter Trees first edition is recorded from bookseller and catalogue listings rather than from a printed bibliography.
